title: Anti-lock Braking (ABS)
summary: Brake harder than the tyres can grip and a wheel locks: the car slides, stops later and will not steer. ABS watches every wheel’s speed and, many times a second, eases and restores the pressure to keep each tyre turning near its best grip.
learningObjectives: Explain what wheel slip is and why a locked wheel brakes worse and cannot steer
Describe how wheel-speed sensors let the ABS computer spot a wheel starting to lock
Explain the hold, release and reapply valve states of an ABS modulator
Compare a locked-wheel stop with an ABS stop on a low-grip road
Know how to brake in an emergency in a car with ABS
beginnerExplanation:
A tyre grips best while it is still turning, just a little slower than the road is passing underneath it. If you brake so hard that the wheel stops turning altogether, the tyre slides. A sliding tyre grips less than a rolling one, and — just as important — it cannot steer the car.

Anti-lock brakes (ABS) stop that from happening. A sensor at every wheel tells a small computer how fast that wheel is turning. If one wheel suddenly slows much faster than the car could, the computer knows it is about to lock. It briefly lets a little pressure out of that wheel’s brake so the wheel can speed up again, then puts the pressure back. It repeats this many times a second.

The result is a wheel that keeps turning while braking hard, close to the tyre’s best grip. On a wet or slippery road the car usually stops shorter than with locked wheels, and you can still steer around an obstacle.

In a car with ABS, an emergency stop is simple: press the pedal hard and keep pressing. A buzzing, pulsing pedal is ABS working — don’t lift off.
technicalExplanation:
Longitudinal slip is s = (v − ωr) / v, where v is vehicle speed and ωr the tyre’s surface speed. Braking force rises with slip to a peak — roughly 10–20 % on many surfaces, the band this lab uses — and then falls towards the sliding value at s = 100 %. Lateral (cornering) force collapses as slip approaches lock, which is why a locked wheel cannot steer.

The ABS controller compares each wheel’s speed (from a tone ring and sensor) with an estimate of vehicle speed built from all the wheels, and also watches wheel deceleration. When slip or deceleration crosses a threshold it commands that wheel’s valves in the hydraulic modulator: HOLD (inlet valve closes, pressure trapped), RELEASE (outlet valve opens to a low-pressure accumulator, pressure falls, the wheel spins back up), then REAPPLY (outlet closes, inlet opens — often in pulses — to rebuild pressure). A return pump sends released fluid back to the master-cylinder side, which the driver feels as pedal pulsation.

The lab shows this as a CONCEPTUAL, stylised cycle: in its illustrative wet-road case the demand of 1.2 g exceeds the 0.7 g grip. Without ABS the wheel locks and the quarter-car slides on μ_slide = 0.5, stopping from 80 km/h in about 51 m; with the stylised cycle averaging about 92 % of peak grip it stops in about 41 m. Real controllers are far more sophisticated, adapting thresholds to the surface, load, cornering and to stability-control demands; on loose gravel or deep snow a locked wheel can sometimes stop shorter by building a wedge of material, which modern systems allow for.

steps.title: The grip limit
steps.beginner: On this wet road the driver presses harder than the tyre can grip. As the pressure rises, the brake asks for more than the road can give.
steps.technical: Brake demand rises with pressure; at 1.2 g of demand against μ_peak g = 0.7 g of grip, the limit is reached partway up the pressure ramp. From here on extra pressure cannot make extra stopping force — it can only make the wheel slip more.

steps.title: Without ABS the wheel locks
steps.beginner: With nothing to stop it, the wheel stops turning while the car keeps going. The tyre slides on the road — watch the sidewall mark freeze while the road keeps moving.
steps.technical: Excess torque spins the wheel down within about a tenth of a second; slip goes to 100 %. Friction falls to the sliding value (μ_slide = 0.5 here), so deceleration drops to 0.5 g. With no rolling there is no lateral grip either: steering input does nothing.

steps.title: A longer slide — and the tyre takes the heat
steps.beginner: The locked car slides to a stop, further than it needed to. Because the disc wasn’t turning, most of the heat went into the sliding tyre, not the brake.
steps.technical: From 80 km/h the locked stop takes about 51 m and 4.6 s. Energy accounting changes too: with the disc stationary, nearly all of ½mv² is dissipated in the tyre’s contact patch, which is how locked wheels grind flat spots into tyres.

steps.title: Sensing that a lock is coming
steps.beginner: With ABS on, the wheel-speed sensor counts the teeth of a ring turning with the hub. When the wheel slows much faster than the car could, the ABS computer knows trouble is starting.
steps.technical: The controller compares each wheel’s speed with a reference vehicle speed and watches wheel deceleration. Rising slip past the target band (or a deceleration spike well above what grip allows) triggers the first HOLD, within a few hundredths of a second of the grip limit.

steps.title: Keeping slip in the band
steps.beginner: ABS now eases the brake off and on, again and again. The wheel never stops turning, so the tyre keeps gripping and the car can still be steered.
steps.technical: In the lab’s conceptual cycle, caliper pressure swings between about 60 % and 105 % of the grip-limit pressure while the master cylinder stays at the driver’s full pressure. Slip stays inside an illustrative 10–20 % band, so average deceleration is close to peak grip.

steps.title: Release: let pressure out
steps.beginner: The ABS unit closes the way in and opens a way out, so some fluid leaves the caliper. The clamp eases and the wheel speeds back up.
steps.technical: RELEASE: inlet valve closed, outlet valve open (amber lamp) to the low-pressure accumulator. Caliper pressure falls while the master side stays high; the wheel’s surface speed recovers towards the vehicle speed and slip falls.

steps.title: Hold and reapply
steps.beginner: Once the wheel is turning properly again, ABS lets the pressure back in and squeezes harder, until the wheel starts to slow too quickly again. Then the cycle repeats.
steps.technical: HOLD (both valves closed) lets the wheel settle; REAPPLY opens the inlet (cyan lamp) to raise caliper pressure again, often in small steps. The pump returns released fluid to the master side — the pedal pulsation drivers feel. Real systems repeat this many times per second; the lab’s stylised cycle runs about six times per second.

steps.title: A shorter, steerable stop
steps.beginner: With ABS the car stopped in a shorter distance and could have been steered all the way. The brake disc, not the tyre, took most of the heat.
steps.technical: In the illustrative wet case the ABS stop takes about 41 m and 3.6 s against 51 m and 4.6 s locked. Most of the energy goes into the brake again; a small share is dissipated by tyre slip.

keyConcepts.definition: How much slower the tyre’s surface is moving than the road beneath it, as a fraction of vehicle speed. 0 % is free rolling; 100 % is a locked, sliding wheel.
A braking tyre grips best at a small amount of slip and less once it slides, so a locked wheel decelerates the car less than one held near the peak.
Each wheel circuit in the modulator has an inlet and an outlet valve. Hold traps the pressure, release lets some out, reapply lets it back in.
A tyre can only produce cornering force while it is rolling. Keeping the wheels turning is what lets an ABS-equipped car steer during an emergency stop.

keyConcepts.term: Stopping distance at the grip limit
keyConcepts.definition: Once braking is limited by grip, the stopping distance depends on the friction the tyres achieve, so holding the tyres near peak grip stops the car shorter than sliding.

misconceptions.myth: ABS always makes the car stop in a shorter distance.
misconceptions.reality: Its main job is to keep the car steerable. On most paved surfaces it also shortens the stop, but on loose gravel or deep snow a locked wheel can sometimes stop shorter by ploughing up material — and ABS cannot add grip that isn’t there, so on ice the stop is still long.

misconceptions.myth: When the pedal starts pulsing and buzzing, something has gone wrong — ease off.
misconceptions.reality: Pulsing and noise mean ABS is working. Keep pressing hard and steer where you want to go; lifting off makes the stop longer.

misconceptions.myth: You should pump the brake pedal in an emergency, even with ABS.
misconceptions.reality: Pumping was a technique for cars without ABS. With ABS, the system modulates far faster and per wheel; your job is to press firmly and keep pressing.

misconceptions.myth: With ABS you can brake as late as you like.
misconceptions.reality: ABS cannot create grip. Stopping distance is still set by speed and the road surface — it grows with the square of speed and is several times longer on ice.

practicalExamples: In an emergency stop in a car with ABS: press the brake hard, keep it pressed through the pulsing, and steer around the hazard if you need to.
An amber ABS warning light means the anti-lock function is off; normal braking usually still works, but have it checked soon and leave more distance meanwhile.
A faulty wheel-speed sensor (often from dirt, damage or a broken wire) is a common cause of an ABS warning light.
On a car without ABS, a skidding stop leaves dark rubber marks on the road; with ABS the marks, if any, are faint and broken.
Mismatched or badly worn tyres reduce the grip ABS has to work with — the system can only hold the tyre near the peak it actually has.

quiz.prompt: The car is doing 20 m/s and the tyre’s surface speed (ωr) is 17 m/s. What is the wheel slip?
quiz.explanation: s = (v − ωr) / v = (20 − 17) / 20 = 0.15, or 15 % — inside the band where many tyres give their best braking grip.

quiz.prompt: Why can’t a car steer while its front wheels are locked?
options: The steering rack locks when the brakes are applied
A sliding tyre produces almost no sideways (cornering) force
The brake caliper stops the wheel from turning left or right
The ABS computer disables the steering
quiz.explanation: Cornering force comes from a rolling tyre’s contact patch deforming as it turns. A locked tyre just slides in the direction the car is moving.

quiz.prompt: In the ABS modulator’s release state, which valves are open?
quiz.explanation: Release closes the inlet (so no more pressure arrives) and opens the outlet, letting fluid out of the caliper so the wheel can spin back up.

quiz.prompt: During an emergency stop the brake pedal pulses and buzzes. What should the driver do?
options: Lift off and pump the pedal
Keep pressing firmly and steer as needed
quiz.explanation: The pulsing is ABS returning fluid and cycling the valves. Keep firm pressure on the pedal and steer; ABS keeps the wheels turning.

quiz.prompt: What does the wheel-speed sensor actually measure?
options: The pressure in the brake line
The temperature of the brake disc
How fast the wheel is turning, from the teeth of a ring passing the sensor
The distance to the car in front
quiz.explanation: Each passing tooth on the tone ring (or magnetic pole in the bearing) produces a pulse; the pulse rate gives wheel speed, from which the computer works out slip.
